## Summary

- Oral Bible translation (OBT) projects record Scripture in a language with no written Bible. The recordings are transcribed by a speech recognition (ASR) model, and the transcripts are used to fine-tune a machine translation (MT) model that drafts the next books.
- With **only Matthew** (the first 10 chapters transcribed by humans) the pipeline drafts held-out Matthew passages at **64.0 passage-level chrF3**.
- Adding books helps modestly. Matthew, Mark and Acts reach **65.6**, and the New Testament except Luke **66.7**, about 2.7 points above Matthew alone.
- **Mark alone (63.6) is nearly as good as Matthew alone**, while Acts alone (60.6) and Romans alone (56.3) are clearly lower.
- The conclusion we draw is that AI drafting is viable for OBT projects even at an early stage, with one gospel recorded. Each score comes from one training run on 17 passages, so differences of about a point or less should be treated as noise.

## The question

An OBT project doesn't start with a written Bible, so an MT model has to learn from what the project has already recorded. How much recorded Scripture is enough for the drafts to be useful? Early in a project there may be a single gospel.

## The pipeline

1. **Speech recognition.** An ASR model (MMS) was trained on human transcriptions of the first 10 chapters of Matthew, and then transcribed the project's recordings of the other books.
2. **Verse segmentation.** The ASR output is running text for each recording, so it was split into verses to line up with the verses of a published Bible.
3. **Machine translation.** NLLB-200 (1.3 billion parameters) was fine-tuned with silnlp on the verse-segmented ASR output for a chosen set of books, aligned verse by verse with a published Bible in a related language. The target and source are two different languages, called Language A and Language B here.
4. **Drafting.** The fine-tuned model translated Matthew 11 to 16 from the published Bible, and the draft was scored against what the project's own speakers said.

<!-- REVIEW: step 1-3 details (ASR trained on Mt. 1-10 transcriptions only; MT trained on ASR output of the listed books; model size; that the segmentation step splits ASR output into verses) are from the experiment configs and the spreadsheet "Experiments with Less Data - MT Evaluation"; please confirm the wording. -->

Each experiment differs only in which books the MT model trained on.

## How it was tested

Every model was scored at its 5,000-step checkpoint on **17 passages of Matthew 11 to 16**, none of which was used to train the ASR or MT models. The reference for each passage is the human transcription of the recording, not a written verse text.

The score is **chrF3**, computed over whole passages.

## Results

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
study.dot_chart(
    "chrF3",
    x_title="Passage-level chrF3 on held-out passages",
    x_range=(50, 70),
)
```

```{python}
study.table(intervals=False, measure_column=False, group_title="MT training books")
```

- **One gospel is enough to start.** Matthew alone gives 64.0. Mark alone gives 63.6, so a different gospel works about equally well.
- **More data helps a little.** Matthew and Acts reach 64.6, adding Mark 65.6, and the New Testament except Luke 66.7. Each step is a gain of about a point or less, within what one run on 17 passages can move.
- **Non-gospel books alone are weaker.** Acts alone (60.6) and Romans alone (56.3) trail the gospels by 3 to 7 points. This study did not test why.
- **Adding Romans to Matthew, Mark and Acts did not help** (65.3 against 65.6), which is a difference well inside the noise.

<!-- REVIEW: 66.69 (New Testament except Luke) is in the spreadsheet but I could not reproduce it from an experiment folder; the other seven scores were re-scored from the experiments and match the sheet. -->

## Limitations

- **One run and 17 passages per setting.** There are no confidence intervals and no repeated runs, so small differences between settings are not established.
- **One language pair and one test passage range.** The results describe one project's language, tested on Matthew 11 to 16. Another language, or the Old Testament, may behave differently.
- **A score is not a judgment of quality.** Whether a chrF3 near 65 makes a draft useful to a translation team was not measured here. "Reasonably good" is our reading, and a team's own assessment should decide.
